newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran leader says Germany must pay for mistakes.
newsitem.headline: Iran leader says Germany must pay for mistakes.

text.p: Iran's supreme spiritual leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei said on Wednesday Germany would have to pay for a row provoked by a Berlin court's ruling that Tehran ordered political killings.

"The German government became the victim of a U.S.-Zionist plot but this does not mitigate its fault...They will have to pay for this error and, in my opinion, the German government has paid and will continue to pay a high price," Khamenei said in a speech carried on Tehran radio.

"The Germans have lost something in this transaction which is not easily won: the trust of the Iranian people. Iran's people have no confidence in Germans anymore," Khamenei told military commanders and personnel on the eve of Iran's Army Day.

Iranian officials have said the row was instigated by Israel and the United States -- Iran's arch-enemies -- to damage Tehran's ties with Bonn, until recently Iran's main trade partner and a rare major Western friend.
The row broke out after the court ruled that top Iranian leaders ordered the 1992 killings of four Kurdish dissidents in Berlin. Iran has repeatedly denied all involvement.

"The (Iranian) government should act wisely and with dignity...Officials should not feel rushed. They should not feel in need of anything at all -- as praise be to God they do not. We do not need anyone," Khamenei said.
He said Iran would not be hurt by any cut in ties with Germany and other European states because the country had become "relatively self-reliant in all fields" over the years.
Iran has responded to the recalling for consultations of all European Union ambassadors, except Greece's, by announcing it would reciprocate.

"I have instructed the foreign ministry to register the actions of these countries carefully, so that we will know how each country reacted...at these trying times," said Khamenei, who has supreme power over all state institutions.

"We will not retreat one step in the face of America's bullying, even if they are able to sever Europe's ties with Iran -- which they will surely fail to do -- or if they create 10 other enemies as strong as Europe against us," he said.
The officers responded with the Islamic rallying cry of "Allahu Akbar" (God is Greatest) and chants of "Death to America" and "Death to Israel".

The ruling was the first time a European court had clearly attributed political responsibility for any of the dozens of assassinations of Iranian opposition figures abroad since the Islamic revolution in 1979.

The court said Iranian leaders including the state president and the religious leader had ordered the killings. But it only mentioned Intelligence Minister Ali Fallahiyan by name. Iran has blamed the slayings on infighting between dissident groups.
Some 3,000 Iranian veterans disabled in Iraqi chemical attacks marched on Germany's embassy in Tehran on Wednesday to protest the court verdict, witnesses said.
It was the fourth demonstration at the barricaded embassy.
Tehran has said court proceedings would begin shortly against 24 German companies accused of having helped Iraq produce chemical weapons during the 1980-88 Iran-Iraq war.
